claim: The labeling and identification of long-range axonal inputs from multiple sources within densely reconstructed electron microscopy (EM) datasets from mammalian brains has been notoriously difficult because of the limited color label space of EM.
source: The labeling and identification of long-range axonal inputs from multiple sources within densely reconstructed electron microscopy (EM) datasets from mammalian brains has been notoriously difficult because of the limited color label space of EM.
evidence: This is a statement about the challenges in the field, supported by the context of existing literature and the motivation for the study.

claim: FluoEM enables identification of multi-color fluorescently labeled axons in dense EM data without the need for artificial fiducial marks or chemical label conversion.
source: Here, we report FluoEM for the identification of multi-color fluorescently labeled axons in dense EM data without the need for artificial fiducial marks or chemical label conversion.
evidence: This is a primary claim about the method's capabilities, supported by the experimental demonstrations in the manuscript.

claim: The FluoEM approach is based on correlated tissue imaging and computational matching of neurite reconstructions.
source: The approach is based on correlated tissue imaging and computational matching of neurite reconstructions, amounting to a virtual color labeling of axons in dense EM circuit data.
evidence: This describes the methodological basis of FluoEM, which is demonstrated throughout the manuscript.

claim: The identification of fluorescent light-microscopically (LM) imaged axons in 3D EM data from mouse cortex is faithfully possible as soon as the EM dataset is about 40–50 µm in extent.
source: We show that the identification of fluorescent light- microscopically (LM) imaged axons in 3D EM data from mouse cortex is faithfully possible as soon as the EM dataset is about 40–50 µm in extent, relying on the unique trajectories of axons in dense mammalian neuropil.
evidence: This claim is supported by the measurements of axonal uniqueness length presented in Figure 2.

claim: FluoEM relies on the unique trajectories of axons in dense mammalian neuropil.
source: We show that the identification of fluorescent light- microscopically (LM) imaged axons in 3D EM data from mouse cortex is faithfully possible as soon as the EM dataset is about 40–50 µm in extent, relying on the unique trajectories of axons in dense mammalian neuropil.
evidence: This is a key principle underlying the FluoEM method, demonstrated by the uniqueness length measurements.

claim: Dense reconstruction of neuronal circuits has become an increasingly realistic goal in the neurosciences thanks to developments in large-scale 3D EM.
source: The dense reconstruction of neuronal circuits has become an increasingly realistic goal in the neurosciences thanks to developments in large-scale 3D EM (Denk and Horstmann, 2004; Bock et al., 2011; Hayworth et al., 2015; Kasthuri et al., 2015; Xu et al., 2017) and circuit reconstruction techniques (Saalfeld et al., 2009; Boergens et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work in the field.

claim: First locally dense neuronal circuits have been mapped using 3D EM techniques.
source: First locally dense neuronal circuits have been mapped using these techniques (Helmstaedter et al., 2013; Kasthuri et al., 2015; Berck et al., 2016; Wanner et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: In mammalian nervous systems, any given local neuronal circuit receives numerous synaptic inputs from distant neuronal sources.
source: However, in mammalian nervous systems, any given local neuronal circuit receives numerous synaptic inputs from distant neuronal sources.
evidence: This is a general statement about mammalian neuroanatomy, supported by established knowledge.

claim: In most layers of the mammalian cortex, the fraction of distal input synapses in a dense local circuit is estimated to comprise 70–90% of all synapses.
source: In most layers of the mammalian cortex, for example, the fraction of distal input synapses in a dense local circuit is estimated to comprise 70–90% of all synapses (Stepanyants et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Subcortical structures such as the striatum or amygdala receive the vast majority of their inputs from distal projection sources.
source: Similarly, subcortical structures as the striatum or amygdala (Figure 1a) receive the vast majority of their inputs from distal projection sources.
evidence: This is supported by reference to Figure 1a and general neuroanatomical knowledge.

claim: 3D EM is still limited to volumes that do not routinely encompass entire mammalian brains.
source: Since 3D EM is still limited to volumes that do not routinely encompass entire mammalian brains, the origin of a large fraction of input synapses remains thus unidentified in current high-resolution connectomic experiments in mammals.
evidence: This is a statement about current technical limitations in the field.

claim: The origin of a large fraction of input synapses remains unidentified in current high-resolution connectomic experiments in mammals.
source: Since 3D EM is still limited to volumes that do not routinely encompass entire mammalian brains, the origin of a large fraction of input synapses remains thus unidentified in current high-resolution connectomic experiments in mammals.
evidence: This is an inference based on the technical limitations of 3D EM.

claim: The labeling of multiple neuronal populations and their axonal projections by fluorescent dyes visible in LM is routine.
source: At the same time, the labeling of multiple neuronal populations and their axonal projections by fluorescent dyes visible in LM is routine (Livet et al., 2007; Mao et al., 2011; D'Souza et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work demonstrating fluorescent labeling techniques.

claim: Direct correlative light- and electron microscopy (CLEM) has been successful for high-resolution subcellular label localization.
source: Such direct correlative light- and electron microscopy (CLEM) has been successful for high-resolution subcellular label localization (Agronskaia et al., 2008; Murphy et al., 2011; Liv et al., 2013) and synaptic identification (Micheva and Smith, 2007; Rah et al., 2013), but can so far not be combined with 3D EM at both resolution and scale allowing for dense large-scale circuit mapping in mammalian neuropil.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior CLEM studies.

claim: Direct CLEM can so far not be combined with 3D EM at both resolution and scale allowing for dense large-scale circuit mapping in mammalian neuropil.
source: Such direct correlative light- and electron microscopy (CLEM) has been successful for high-resolution subcellular label localization (Agronskaia et al., 2008; Murphy et al., 2011; Liv et al., 2013) and synaptic identification (Micheva and Smith, 2007; Rah et al., 2013), but can so far not be combined with 3D EM at both resolution and scale allowing for dense large-scale circuit mapping in mammalian neuropil.
evidence: This is a statement about current technical limitations, based on knowledge of the field.

claim: En-bloc immunolabeling in conjunction with EM is limited to thin tissue slices.
source: Similarly, en-bloc immunolabeling in conjunction with EM is limited to thin tissue slices (Faulk and Taylor, 1971; Pallotto et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Approaches to interlace EM and LM imaging on alternating tissue slices impede dense EM-based circuit reconstruction in mammalian nervous tissue.
source: Approaches to interlace EM and LM imaging on alternating tissue slices, though successfully applied in invertebrates (Shahidi et al., 2015), impede dense EM-based circuit reconstruction in mammalian nervous tissue.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of alternating slice approaches, with a citation to work in invertebrates.

claim: Methods to obtain electron-dense labels in a subset of neurons have been developed over the decades based on induced axonal degeneration.
source: Rather, methods to obtain electron-dense labels in a subset of neurons have been developed over the decades based on induced axonal degeneration (Gray and Hamlyn, 1962; Colonnier, 1964; White, 1978), introduction of HRP (Hersch and White, 1981; Hamos et al., 1985; Horikawa and Armstrong, 1988; Anderson et al., 1994a; Anderson et al., 1994b; Markram et al., 1997; da Costa and Martin, 2011) or fluorophores (Maranto, 1982; Grabenbauer et al., 2005; Knott et al., 2009) into a subset of neurons which could be utilized to create electron contrast via enzymatic or photo-oxidative DAB polymerization.
evidence: This is supported by extensive citations to historical methods.

claim: Recent improvements enabled the genetically targeted expression of electron-dense labels in diverse cellular compartments.
source: More recent improvements enabled the genetically targeted expression of electron-dense labels in diverse cellular compartments, potentially allowing to encode multiple label classes in a single EM experiment (Shu et al., 2011; Martell et al., 2012; Atasoy et al., 2014; Lam et al., 2015; Joesch et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent work on genetically encoded EM labels.

claim: Generating multiple electron-dense label classes in the very same experiment while ensuring ultrastructural preservation is challenging.
source: However, generating multiple electron-dense label classes in the very same experiment while ensuring ultrastructural preservation is challenging and to our knowledge has been accomplished in Drosophila (Lin et al., 2016) but so far not in mammals.
evidence: This is a statement about technical challenges, with a citation to work in Drosophila.

claim: Multiple electron-dense label classes have been accomplished in Drosophila but so far not in mammals.
source: However, generating multiple electron-dense label classes in the very same experiment while ensuring ultrastructural preservation is challenging and to our knowledge has been accomplished in Drosophila (Lin et al., 2016) but so far not in mammals.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to work in Drosophila and knowledge of the mammalian field.

claim: Methods to directly co-register light microscopic labels in axons and dendrites with 3D EM data have been restricted to local volumes of up to 10 µm on a side.
source: Methods to directly co-register light microscopic labels in axons and dendrites with 3D EM data (Bishop et al., 2011; Maco et al., 2013; Gala et al., 2017) have been restricted to local volumes of up to 10 µm on a side, using LM-burnt fiducial marks visible in EM; these do not scale to the large volumes required for neuronal circuit reconstruction (sized hundreds of micrometers per dimension, that is at least 1000-fold larger).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior co-registration methods.

claim: Direct co-alignment between fluorescently labeled cell bodies and EM data has been routinely applied.
source: Direct co-alignment between fluorescently labeled cell bodies and EM data has been routinely applied (Bock et al., 2011; Briggman et al., 2011; Lee et al., 2016; Tsang et al., 2018), but provides LM-to-EM alignment only at a coarse scale that does not allow for the identification of single axons.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on cell body alignment.

claim: Direct co-alignment between fluorescently labeled cell bodies and EM data provides LM-to-EM alignment only at a coarse scale that does not allow for the identification of single axons.
source: Direct co-alignment between fluorescently labeled cell bodies and EM data has been routinely applied (Bock et al., 2011; Briggman et al., 2011; Lee et al., 2016; Tsang et al., 2018), but provides LM-to-EM alignment only at a coarse scale that does not allow for the identification of single axons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the limitations of coarse alignment methods.

claim: Current computational approaches are challenged when attempting submicron registration precision of neurites in volumes required for connectomics.
source: Apart from the experimental limitations currently hampering the use of multi-color labels in large 3D EM data, current computational approaches are challenged when attempting submicron registration precision of neurites in volumes required for connectomics (~106 µm3 or larger).
evidence: This is a statement about computational challenges in the field.

claim: Previously proposed multi-modal graph-based neurite registration can in principle be used for LM-to-EM morphological matching, but did not yet scale to graphs of thousands or tens of thousands of nodes as required for connectomics.
source: Previously proposed multi-modal graph-based neurite registration (Serradell et al., 2012; Fua and Knott, 2015; Serradell et al., 2015) can in principle be used for LM-to-EM morphological matching, but did not yet scale to graphs of thousands or tens of thousands of nodes as required for connectomics.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior computational methods and their limitations.

claim: FluoEM exploits the availability of locally dense neurite reconstructions in current volume EM.
source: Instead of directly attempting alignment of LM-labeled axons to the EM dataset at the nanometer scale, we exploit the availability of locally dense neurite reconstructions in current volume EM.
evidence: This describes a key principle of the FluoEM method.

claim: In FluoEM, the alignment problem can be re-formulated as identifying the most likely axon (out of all axons, reconstructed in EM) that best explains an LM-imaged axonal fluorescence signal.
source: Here, the alignment problem can be re-formulated as identifying the most likely axon (out of all axons, reconstructed in EM) that best explains an LM-imaged axonal fluorescence signal.
evidence: This describes the conceptual basis of the FluoEM approach.

claim: The FluoEM workflow comprised acquisition of a 3D fluorescence-LM dataset from a given piece of tissue.
source: The FluoEM workflow (Figure 1b) comprised the following steps: acquisition of a 3D fluorescence-LM dataset from a given piece of tissue; 3D imaging of that very same piece of tissue in the electron microscope; reconstruction of the fluorescently labeled axons in the LM data; reconstruction of locally all axons in small subvolumes of the EM data; computational determination of the most likely EM axons that explain the LM signal.
evidence: This describes the experimental workflow, illustrated in Figure 1b.

claim: The FluoEM workflow comprised 3D imaging of that very same piece of tissue in the electron microscope.
source: The FluoEM workflow (Figure 1b) comprised the following steps: acquisition of a 3D fluorescence-LM dataset from a given piece of tissue; 3D imaging of that very same piece of tissue in the electron microscope; reconstruction of the fluorescently labeled axons in the LM data; reconstruction of locally all axons in small subvolumes of the EM data; computational determination of the most likely EM axons that explain the LM signal.
evidence: This describes the experimental workflow, illustrated in Figure 1b.

claim: The FluoEM workflow comprised reconstruction of the fluorescently labeled axons in the LM data.
source: The FluoEM workflow (Figure 1b) comprised the following steps: acquisition of a 3D fluorescence-LM dataset from a given piece of tissue; 3D imaging of that very same piece of tissue in the electron microscope; reconstruction of the fluorescently labeled axons in the LM data; reconstruction of locally all axons in small subvolumes of the EM data; computational determination of the most likely EM axons that explain the LM signal.
evidence: This describes the experimental workflow, illustrated in Figure 1b.

claim: The FluoEM workflow comprised reconstruction of locally all axons in small subvolumes of the EM data.
source: The FluoEM workflow (Figure 1b) comprised the following steps: acquisition of a 3D fluorescence-LM dataset from a given piece of tissue; 3D imaging of that very same piece of tissue in the electron microscope; reconstruction of the fluorescently labeled axons in the LM data; reconstruction of locally all axons in small subvolumes of the EM data; computational determination of the most likely EM axons that explain the LM signal.
evidence: This describes the experimental workflow, illustrated in Figure 1b.

claim: The FluoEM workflow comprised computational determination of the most likely EM axons that explain the LM signal.
source: The FluoEM workflow (Figure 1b) comprised the following steps: acquisition of a 3D fluorescence-LM dataset from a given piece of tissue; 3D imaging of that very same piece of tissue in the electron microscope; reconstruction of the fluorescently labeled axons in the LM data; reconstruction of locally all axons in small subvolumes of the EM data; computational determination of the most likely EM axons that explain the LM signal.
evidence: This describes the experimental workflow, illustrated in Figure 1b.

claim: Blood vessels were used as intrinsic fiducials in the neuropil to obtain a coarse co-registration between LM and EM.
source: In a first step, we used blood vessels as intrinsic fiducials in the neuropil to obtain a coarse co-registration between LM and EM (Figure 1b).
evidence: This describes a methodological step, illustrated in Figure 1b.

claim: Adeno-associated viruses expressing fluorescent markers were injected into the primary motor cortex (M1) and the secondary somatosensory cortex (S2) of a 28-day-old mouse.
source: We first performed a fluorescence imaging experiment (Figure 2a–c) in which we injected adeno-associated viruses expressing fluorescent markers into the primary motor cortex (M1; virus expressing the green marker eGFP) and the secondary somatosensory cortex (S2; virus expressing the red marker tdTomato) of a 28-day-old mouse, followed by transcardial perfusion and tissue extraction at 46 days of age.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure, illustrated in Figure 2a.

claim: A confocal laser scanning microscope was used to acquire a dataset sized (828 × 828 × 75) µm3 at a voxel size of (104 × 104 × 444) nm3 from layer 1 of cortex.
source: Using a confocal laser scanning microscope, we then acquired a dataset sized (828 × 828 × 75) µm3 at a voxel size of (104 × 104 × 444) nm3 from layer 1 of a part of cortex in which both of these projections converged (located to lateral parietal association cortex (LPtA), Figure 2b).
evidence: This describes the imaging parameters, with reference to Figure 2b.

claim: All axons traversing a (40 × 40 × 48) µm3 bounding box in the LM image dataset were 3D-reconstructed using webKnossos.
source: We then 3D-reconstructed all axons traversing a (40 × 40 × 48) µm3 bounding box in this LM image dataset using our annotation tool webKnossos (Boergens et al., 2017) and measured the length over which the axons were faithfully reconstructable as judged by expert annotators (for this we asked the annotators to stop reconstructing whenever they encountered a location of any ambiguity, the loss of axon continuity or an unclear branching).
evidence: This describes the reconstruction procedure using webKnossos.

claim: Ninety-five percent of axons were reconstructable above 20 µm length.
source: Ninety-five percent of axons were reconstructable above 20 µm length, some for up to 200 µm (Figure 2c, independent reconstruction by two experts).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the reconstruction analysis, shown in Figure 2c.

claim: A 3D EM dataset sized (130 x 110 x 85) µm3 at a voxel size of (11.24 x 11.24 x 30) nm3 was acquired from layer 1 of LPtA cortex using SBEM.
source: For this, we acquired a 3D EM dataset sized (130 x 110 x 85) µm3 at a voxel size of (11.24 x 11.24 x 30) nm3 from layer 1 of LPtA cortex (Figure 2d,e) using SBEM (Denk and Horstmann, 2004) and reconstructed all n = 220 axons that traversed a cubic bounding box of size (5 x 5 x 5) µm3 in the center of the dataset (Figure 2e, blue box).
evidence: This describes the EM imaging parameters, with reference to Figure 2d,e.

claim: All n = 220 axons that traversed a cubic bounding box of size (5 x 5 x 5) µm3 in the center of the EM dataset were reconstructed.
source: For this, we acquired a 3D EM dataset sized (130 x 110 x 85) µm3 at a voxel size of (11.24 x 11.24 x 30) nm3 from layer 1 of LPtA cortex (Figure 2d,e) using SBEM (Denk and Horstmann, 2004) and reconstructed all n = 220 axons that traversed a cubic bounding box of size (5 x 5 x 5) µm3 in the center of the dataset (Figure 2e, blue box).
evidence: This describes the dense reconstruction in EM, shown in Figure 2e.

claim: The uniqueness length per axon in layer 1 was 22 ± 10 µm (mean ± s.d., range 7 – 78 µm, n = 220 axons).
source: The uniqueness length per axon was 22 ± 10 µm (mean ± s.d., range 7 – 78 µm, n = 220 axons); after 31, 35, 41 and 69 µm, 85%, 90%, 95% and 98% of axons had no other axon in their proximity, respectively.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement of axonal uniqueness from the EM data.

claim: After 35 µm, 90% of axons in layer 1 had no other axon in their proximity.
source: The uniqueness length per axon was 22 ± 10 µm (mean ± s.d., range 7 – 78 µm, n = 220 axons); after 31, 35, 41 and 69 µm, 85%, 90%, 95% and 98% of axons had no other axon in their proximity, respectively.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement of axonal uniqueness from the EM data.

claim: An additional fluorescence channel was acquired to image blood vessels using DiD, a lipophilic dye.
source: For this, we continued the experiment described above (Figure 2a) and acquired an additional fluorescence channel to image blood vessels (during perfusion, the rinsing solution was supplemented with DiD, a lipophilic dye for blood vessel staining with fluorescence in the far red spectrum, around 650 nm).
evidence: This describes an experimental procedure for blood vessel labeling.

claim: A slightly modified version of the standard volume EM staining protocol was applied to the tissue block.
source: Then we applied a slightly modified version of our standard volume EM staining protocol (Hua et al., 2015) to the tissue block (see Materials and methods), embedded and mounted the sample and imaged it using SBEM (Denk and Horstmann, 2004) (Figure 3a).
evidence: This describes the EM sample preparation, with reference to a prior protocol.

claim: EM images with a large field of view (dataset dimensions (1500 × 1000 × 10) µm3) were acquired at lower resolution of (270 × 270 × 200) nm3.
source: We first acquired EM images with a large field of view (dataset dimensions (1500 × 1000 × 10) µm3) at lower resolution of (270 × 270 × 200) nm3 to identify the location of the LM-imaged dataset relative to the EM imaged sample (Figure 3b,c).
evidence: This describes the low-resolution EM imaging parameters.

claim: The pattern of superficial blood vessels was used as coarse alignment fiducials.
source: For this, we used the pattern of superficial blood vessels as coarse alignment fiducials (Figure 3d,e).
evidence: This describes the alignment strategy, illustrated in Figure 3d,e.

claim: A high-resolution 3D EM dataset sized (130 × 110 × 85) µm3 at a voxel size of (11.24 × 11.24 × 30) nm3 was acquired.
source: We then acquired a high-resolution 3D EM dataset sized (130 × 110 × 85) µm3 at a voxel size of (11.24 × 11.24 × 30) nm3 in a region previously imaged using LM with suitable fluorescent labeling density (Figure 3c,g).
evidence: This describes the high-resolution EM imaging parameters.

claim: Blood vessels were reconstructed in both the high-resolution EM dataset and the corresponding LM volume.
source: In both the high-resolution EM dataset and the corresponding LM volume we then reconstructed the blood vessels (Figure 3h,i) and annotated their branch points as control points for fitting a coarse affine transformation ATBV from the LM to the high-resolution EM dataset (Figure 3h–n, n = 7 control points).
evidence: This describes the reconstruction and alignment procedure, shown in Figure 3h,i.

claim: Blood vessel branch points were annotated as control points (n = 7) for fitting a coarse affine transformation from the LM to the high-resolution EM dataset.
source: In both the high-resolution EM dataset and the corresponding LM volume we then reconstructed the blood vessels (Figure 3h,i) and annotated their branch points as control points for fitting a coarse affine transformation ATBV from the LM to the high-resolution EM dataset (Figure 3h–n, n = 7 control points).
evidence: This describes the alignment procedure using control points.

claim: The precision of the coarse alignment was 2.7 ± 1.1 µm (mean ± s.d., n = 7, median = 2.7 µm).
source: To estimate the precision of this coarse alignment, we measured its residuals (Figure 3o; 2.7 ± 1.1 µm, mean ± s.d., n = 7, median = 2.7 µm).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement of alignment precision, shown in Figure 3o.

claim: An axon next to a blood vessel in the LM data was chosen for the first LM-to-EM match.
source: We chose an axon next to a blood vessel in the LM data (Figure 4a).
evidence: This describes the selection of the first axon for matching, shown in Figure 4a.

claim: The axon was skeleton-reconstructed at the LM level using webKnossos with a path length of 105 µm.
source: The axon was skeleton-reconstructed at the LM level (Figure 4b) using webKnossos (Boergens et al., 2017). We then transformed this LM reconstruction (path length of 105 µm) to the EM dataset using the coarse transformation ATBV based on blood vessel correspondence as determined before (Figure 4c).
evidence: This describes the reconstruction and transformation procedure.

claim: Based solely on the coarse transformation, an identification of the corresponding axon at the EM level was impossible.
source: Evidently, based solely on this coarse transformation, an identification of the corresponding axon at the EM level was impossible (Figure 4d).
evidence: This is an observation from the alignment attempt, shown in Figure 4d.

claim: A cubic region sized (5 µm)3 was defined in the EM data next to the blood vessel at which the LM reconstruction had been seeded.
source: Rather, we then defined a cubic region sized (5 µm)3 in the EM data next to the blood vessel at which the LM reconstruction had been seeded (Figure 4e,f) and reconstructed all axons that traversed that region in the EM dataset (Figure 4g, n = 193 axons).
evidence: This describes the search volume definition, shown in Figure 4e,f.

claim: All axons that traversed the cubic region in the EM dataset were reconstructed (n = 193 axons).
source: Rather, we then defined a cubic region sized (5 µm)3 in the EM data next to the blood vessel at which the LM reconstruction had been seeded (Figure 4e,f) and reconstructed all axons that traversed that region in the EM dataset (Figure 4g, n = 193 axons).
evidence: This describes the dense reconstruction in the search volume, shown in Figure 4g.

claim: A spherical search kernel with 5 µm radius was used to determine which EM-reconstructed axons were within the surround of the transformed LM-reconstructed axon.
source: We then used a spherical search kernel with 5 µm radius (Figure 2f) to determine which of the 193 EM-reconstructed axons were within that surround of the transformed LM-reconstructed axon along all of its trajectory (Figure 4h,i).
evidence: This describes the matching algorithm, with reference to Figure 2f and shown in Figure 4h,i.

claim: Beyond a distance of 42 µm along the transformed LM axon, only one candidate EM-reconstructed axon remained persistently within the search kernel.
source: Beyond a distance of 42 µm along the transformed LM axon, only one candidate EM-reconstructed axon remained persistently within the search kernel (Figure 4i).
evidence: This is a result from the matching procedure, shown in Figure 4i.

claim: Axonal varicosities were identified in the EM data for the matched axon.
source: We first investigated the detailed morphology of this axon and identified axonal varicosities in the EM data.
evidence: This describes the validation procedure for the match.

claim: Varicosities visible in the LM data were reconstructed and overlaid with EM varicosities.
source: We then reconstructed the varicosities visible in the LM data and overlaid both (Figure 4j).
evidence: This describes the validation procedure, shown in Figure 4j.

claim: The distance between LM and EM varicosities was 0.7 µm ± 0.6 (mean ± s.d., n = 11).
source: The similarity was visually striking (distance between LM and EM varicosities, 0.7 µm ± 0.6 (mean ± s.d., n = 11); distance between LM and random EM varicosity distributions: 4.9 µm ± 2.1, (mean ± s.d., n = 11 varicosities, n = 105 draws, p < 10−5, Randomization test, Figure 4—figure supplement 1)).
evidence: This is a quantitative validation of the match.

claim: The distance between LM and random EM varicosity distributions was 4.9 µm ± 2.1 (mean ± s.d., n = 11 varicosities, n = 105 draws, p < 10−5).
source: The similarity was visually striking (distance between LM and EM varicosities, 0.7 µm ± 0.6 (mean ± s.d., n = 11); distance between LM and random EM varicosity distributions: 4.9 µm ± 2.1, (mean ± s.d., n = 11 varicosities, n = 105 draws, p < 10−5, Randomization test, Figure 4—figure supplement 1)).
evidence: This is a statistical validation of the match using randomization test.

claim: Each matched axon provided additional registration constraints beyond the initial blood-vessel-based constraints.
source: Since each matched axon provided additional registration constraints beyond the initial blood-vessel-based constraints, we could now use each matched axon to further refine an elastic-free-form LM-to-EM transformation using the matched varicosities, branchpoints and other prominent structural features of the axons seen in both LM and EM (Figure 4b,k).
evidence: This describes the iterative refinement strategy.

claim: While the first match involved the reconstruction of 193 axons, subsequent matches were successful after only several or even one reconstruction attempt.
source: While the first match involved the reconstruction of 193 axons, the subsequent matches were successful after only several or even one reconstruction attempt and a few minutes of reconstruction time (Figure 5e).
evidence: This is a comparison of work effort, shown in Figure 5e.

claim: A total of 38 axons were matched (27 in the red fluorescence channel, 11 in the green channel), using a total of 284 control points.
source: Using this strategy, we matched a total of 38 axons (27 in the red fluorescence channel, 11 in the green channel), using a total of 284 control points (7.5 ± 3.8 cps per axon (mean ± s.d), Figure 5g).
evidence: This is a summary of the matching results, shown in Figure 5g.

claim: The residual registration error was reduced from 725 ± 408 nm (mean ± s.d) for affine registration to 487 ± 290 nm (mean ± s.d) for free-form registration.
source: Compared to the affine registration, the residual registration error was reduced by one third from 725 ± 408 nm (mean ± s.d) to 487 ± 290 nm (mean ± s.d, Figure 5h; Figure 5—figure supplement 1), thus about six-fold smaller than in the blood vessel based coarse pre-alignment obtained before (cf. Figure 3o; see Figure 5i for dependence on control point number).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of registration precision, shown in Figure 5h.

claim: About 90% (86 ± 3%, mean ± s.d, n = 7 LM image planes) of the fluorescent voxels were explained by the matched EM axons in the depth range of 17–20 µm.
source: We found that in fact about 90% (86 ± 3%, mean ± s.d, n = 7 LM image planes) of the fluorescent voxels were explained by the matched EM axons in this depth range (Figure 5o).
evidence: This is a quantitative measure of matching completeness, shown in Figure 5o.

claim: Investing a total of 195 work hours, the EM equivalents of 38 fluorescently labeled axons in two fluorescence channels (total axonal path length of 4.6 mm) were obtained.
source: In summary, investing a total of 195 work hours (178.8 hr for the first axon; 16.6 hr for the remaining axons) we obtained the EM equivalents of 38 fluorescently labeled axons in two fluorescence channels (total axonal path length of 4.6 mm).
evidence: This is a summary of the work effort and results.

claim: The total reported time included LM-to-EM matching (181.1 hr), full axon reconstruction in EM (4.8 hr) and control point placement in LM and EM (9.5 hr).
source: The total reported time included LM-to-EM matching (181.1 hr), full axon reconstruction in EM (4.8 hr) and control point placement in LM and EM (9.5 hr).
evidence: This is a breakdown of the work effort.

claim: When using varicosities as a search criterion for the initial match, the invested total time was only 30.3 min.
source: In fact, when asking a second independent expert to perform the first LM-to-EM axonal match by also using varicosities as a search criterion, the invested total time was only 30.3 min for the initial match (7.5 min for EM-to-LM matching, 6.8 min full axon reconstruction in EM, 16.0 min control point placement in LM and EM).
evidence: This demonstrates an alternative, more efficient matching strategy.

claim: About 70% of axons (27 of 38) were correctly reconstructed at the LM level.
source: We found that while a large fraction of axons were reconstructed faithfully at the LM level (27 of 38 axons, 71%), in 29% of cases the LM reconstruction contained an error (Figure 6f).
evidence: This is a quantitative assessment of LM reconstruction accuracy, shown in Figure 6f.

claim: In 29% of cases, the LM reconstruction contained an error.
source: We found that while a large fraction of axons were reconstructed faithfully at the LM level (27 of 38 axons, 71%), in 29% of cases the LM reconstruction contained an error (Figure 6f).
evidence: This is a quantitative assessment of LM reconstruction errors, shown in Figure 6f.

claim: The largest fraction of LM reconstruction errors was related to incorrectly terminated reconstructions (38%).
source: The largest fraction of errors was related to incorrectly terminated reconstructions ('stop', 38%, Figure 6b,f), followed by an incorrect continuation of the LM-reconstructed axon at locations where multiple fluorescent axons overlapped (31% of errors, Figure 6c,f).
evidence: This is a breakdown of error types, shown in Figure 6f.

claim: Incorrect continuation of the LM-reconstructed axon at locations where multiple fluorescent axons overlapped accounted for 31% of errors.
source: The largest fraction of errors was related to incorrectly terminated reconstructions ('stop', 38%, Figure 6b,f), followed by an incorrect continuation of the LM-reconstructed axon at locations where multiple fluorescent axons overlapped (31% of errors, Figure 6c,f).
evidence: This is a breakdown of error types, shown in Figure 6f.

claim: Missed branches accounted for 23% of LM reconstruction errors.
source: Furthermore, missed (23%) and added (8%) branches occurred (Figure 6d,e,f).
evidence: This is a breakdown of error types, shown in Figure 6f.

claim: Added branches accounted for 8% of LM reconstruction errors.

evidence: This is a breakdown of error types, shown in Figure 6f.

source: Labeling density was 1.2 ± 0.2% (mean ± s.d., n = 115 planes) for the tdTomato channel and 1.4 ± 0.4% (mean ± s.d., n = 115 planes) for the eGFP channel; error rates evaluated separately for axons in each channel were 30% of axons (tdTomato) and 27% of axons (eGFP), respectively.

claim: 255 axonal varicosities were identified in the LM data.
source: We then identified 255 axonal varicosities in the LM data and investigated their ultrastructure at the EM level based on the successfully matched axonal counterparts (Figure 6a,g–o).
evidence: This describes the varicosity analysis.

claim: 63% of LM varicosities (n = 161 of 255) correspond to presynaptic boutons.
source: As the examples indicate (Figure 6g–m), many varicosities in the LM in fact correspond to presynaptic boutons (63%, n = 161 of 255, Figure 6h,k,l).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the varicosity analysis, shown in Figure 6.

claim: A substantial fraction of LM-varicosities (n = 54) are without evidence for a presynaptic specialization and instead contain only mitochondria.
source: A substantial fraction of LM-varicosities, however, are without evidence for a presynaptic specialization and instead contain only mitochondria (n = 54, Figure 6g,j), or are hollow thickenings (n = 39, Figure 6i) or myelinated (n = 1, Figure 6m).
evidence: This is a result from the ultrastructural analysis of varicosities.

claim: Some LM-varicosities are hollow thickenings (n = 39).
source: A substantial fraction of LM-varicosities, however, are without evidence for a presynaptic specialization and instead contain only mitochondria (n = 54, Figure 6g,j), or are hollow thickenings (n = 39, Figure 6i) or myelinated (n = 1, Figure 6m).
evidence: This is a result from the ultrastructural analysis of varicosities.

claim: The inference of synaptic boutons from LM varicosities was dependent on the size of the LM varicosity.
source: Notably, while the inference of synaptic boutons from LM varicosities was dependent on the size of the LM varicosity (Figure 6n) with larger varicosities more likely synaptic, there was no LM varicosity size range that allowed unequivocal inference of a synapse from the LM morphology (Figure 6n,o).
evidence: This is an analysis of the relationship between varicosity size and synapse presence, shown in Figure 6n.

claim: Larger varicosities were more likely synaptic.
source: Notably, while the inference of synaptic boutons from LM varicosities was dependent on the size of the LM varicosity (Figure 6n) with larger varicosities more likely synaptic, there was no LM varicosity size range that allowed unequivocal inference of a synapse from the LM morphology (Figure 6n,o).
evidence: This is an analysis result shown in Figure 6n.

claim: There was no LM varicosity size range that allowed unequivocal inference of a synapse from the LM morphology.
source: Notably, while the inference of synaptic boutons from LM varicosities was dependent on the size of the LM varicosity (Figure 6n) with larger varicosities more likely synaptic, there was no LM varicosity size range that allowed unequivocal inference of a synapse from the LM morphology (Figure 6n,o).
evidence: This is an analysis result shown in Figure 6n,o.

claim: A second correlated imaging experiment was conducted in layer 1 of mouse S1 cortex.
source: Finally, in order to assure the reproducibility of FluoEM, we conducted a second correlated imaging experiment in layer 1 of mouse S1 cortex (LM dataset sized (1027 × 820 × 84) µm3, EM dataset sized (155 × 135 × 50) µm3, Figure 6p–q), in which we successfully matched 15 axons between LM and EM as a proof of principle.
evidence: This describes the reproduction experiment, shown in Figure 6p–q.

claim: 15 axons were successfully matched between LM and EM in the second experiment.
source: Finally, in order to assure the reproducibility of FluoEM, we conducted a second correlated imaging experiment in layer 1 of mouse S1 cortex (LM dataset sized (1027 × 820 × 84) µm3, EM dataset sized (155 × 135 × 50) µm3, Figure 6p–q), in which we successfully matched 15 axons between LM and EM as a proof of principle.
evidence: This is a result from the reproduction experiment.

claim: The total time investment for the second matching experiment was 10 hr.
source: The total time investment (Figure 6r) for the second matching experiment was 10 hr, which included LM-to-EM axon matching (1.3 hr), full EM-based axon reconstruction (2.4 hr) and LM-EM control point placement (6.5 hr).
evidence: This is a summary of work effort for the reproduction experiment, shown in Figure 6r.

claim: One key prerequisite for FluoEM is the uniqueness of axonal trajectories in dense neuropil.
source: One key prerequisite for FluoEM is the uniqueness of axonal trajectories in dense neuropil.
evidence: This is a statement about the fundamental principle underlying FluoEM.

claim: For a broad range of cortical and subcortical nervous tissue, FluoEM can be applied on the spatial scales described.
source: For a broad range of cortical and subcortical nervous tissue (basal ganglia, thalamus, hypothalamus, nuclei of the brain stem etc.) in which locally dense circuits coexist with incoming projection axons from distant sources, FluoEM can be applied on the spatial scales described here.
evidence: This is a statement about the applicability of FluoEM, based on the demonstrated principles.

claim: Cases in which dense neuropil contains highly anisotropic axons will likely imply a longer scale on which axonal trajectories become unique.
source: Cases in which dense neuropil contains highly anisotropic axons (for example axon bundles in the white matter of mammalian brains) will likely imply a longer scale on which axonal trajectories become unique, and therefore require longer reconstruction lengths in the fluorescence data.
evidence: This is a speculation about the limitations of FluoEM in certain tissue types.

claim: FluoEM is not restricted to the combination with SBEM.
source: Since FluoEM only relies on the underlying geometry of axonal trajectories, which we have shown to be unique on scales achievable with all current 3D EM techniques (Figure 2g–k), FluoEM is not restricted to the combination with SBEM.
evidence: This is an inference based on the principle of axonal uniqueness.

claim: Other 3D EM imaging approaches, especially FIB-SEM and ATUM-SEM, will be useable for the FluoEM approach.
source: Rather, other 3D EM imaging approaches, especially FIB-SEM (Heymann et al., 2006; Knott et al., 2008; Hayworth et al., 2015; Xu et al., 2017) and ATUM-SEM (Schalek et al., 2011; Kasthuri et al., 2015) that provide faithful axonal reconstructions over at least about 40–50 µm extent in three dimensions will be useable for the presented approach.
evidence: This is an inference about the compatibility of FluoEM with other EM techniques, supported by citations.

claim: FluoEM in principle allows the identification of as many axonal projection sources in a single connectomic experiment as can be encoded at the light-microscopic level.
source: While FluoEM in principle allows the identification of as many axonal projection sources in a single connectomic experiment as can be encoded at the light-microscopic level, it is practically limited by the number of fluorescence channels that can be acquired in sequence without exerting damage to the tissue.
evidence: This is a statement about the theoretical capacity of FluoEM.

claim: FluoEM is practically limited by the number of fluorescence channels that can be acquired in sequence without exerting damage to the tissue.
source: While FluoEM in principle allows the identification of as many axonal projection sources in a single connectomic experiment as can be encoded at the light-microscopic level, it is practically limited by the number of fluorescence channels that can be acquired in sequence without exerting damage to the tissue.
evidence: This is a statement about the practical limitations of FluoEM.

claim: Tissue exposed to 2 hr of continuous LM imaging with acquisition of three parallel fluorescence channels was still well usable for subsequent 3D EM circuit reconstruction.
source: In our experiments, tissue exposed to 2 hr of continuous LM imaging with acquisition of three parallel fluorescence channels was still well usable for subsequent 3D EM circuit reconstruction.
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments about tissue preservation.

claim: In FluoEM, it is not necessary to image the axons of interest in their entirety at the LM level.
source: To acquire more fluorescence channels without increasing the local photon dose in the tissue, one can exploit the fact that in FluoEM, it is not necessary to image the axons of interest in their entirety at the LM level.
evidence: This is an inference about the flexibility of the FluoEM approach.

claim: It is sufficient to LM-image volumes of 40–50 µm in extent, as long as all axons of interest pass through that volume.
source: Rather, it is sufficient to LM-image volumes of 40–50 µm in extent, as long as all axons of interest pass through that volume, and to reconstruct the complete axons in EM.
evidence: This is an inference based on the uniqueness length measurements.

claim: A setting in which the volume of interest is split into several subvolumes could multiplex the color range of FluoEM without increasing the exposure time in the LM step.
source: Therefore, a setting in which the volume of interest is split into several subvolumes, in each of which a limited number of fluorescence channels is acquired, could multiplex the color range of FluoEM (Figure 7a–b) without increasing the exposure time in the LM step.
evidence: This is a proposed strategy for extending FluoEM, illustrated in Figure 7a–b.

claim: In LM imaging of mammalian nervous tissue, labeling density of axons poses a notorious limitation as long as axonal trajectories were to be reconstructed from the LM data.
source: In LM imaging of mammalian nervous tissue, labeling density of axons poses a notorious limitation as long as axonal trajectories were to be reconstructed from the LM data (labeling more than about 1 in 1000 to 10,000 axons impedes reconstruction (Helmstaedter, 2013); and LM reconstruction errors may increase substantially with increased labeling density, see Figure 6b–f).
evidence: This is a statement about limitations in LM imaging, supported by citation and data.

claim: With FluoEM, labeling density is only limited by the need to follow axons over the uniqueness length.
source: With FluoEM, labeling density is only limited by the need to follow axons over the uniqueness length (Figures 2 and 3).
evidence: This is an inference about the advantages of FluoEM regarding labeling density.

claim: A setting in which one fluorescence channel contains sparsely labeled axons to provide an accurate pre-alignment, and the other fluorescence channels are densely labeled is a possible solution.
source: Since this depends on the overall alignment precision (Figure 2k), a setting in which one fluorescence channel contains sparsely labeled axons to provide an accurate pre-alignment (see Figure 5g,h), and the other fluorescence channels are densely labeled is a possible solution, in which LM-reconstructable stretches of axons as short as 5 µm would be sufficient for co-registration (Figures 2k and 5h).
evidence: This is a proposed strategy for optimizing FluoEM, based on the alignment precision analysis.

claim: In settings where axonal varicosities can be used as additional constraints on the matching, the LM-to-EM match consumed about 20–30 min per axon.
source: In settings where axonal varicosities can be used as additional constraints on the matching (Figure 5a–d), the LM-to-EM match consumed about 20–30 min per axon (including the full EM reconstruction of the axon and the placement of control points).
evidence: This is a summary of work effort when using varicosities.

claim: A full matching of a sparsely stained volume sized (1 × 1 × 0.1) mm3 would likely consume about 5300 work hours in FluoEM.
source: With this, a full matching of a sparsely stained volume sized (1 × 1 × 0.1) mm3, for example a large area of layer one in the mouse neocortex, would thus likely consume about 5300 work hours in FluoEM (using webKnossos (Boergens et al., 2017), see Materials and methods for estimates).
evidence: This is an extrapolation of work effort for larger volumes.

claim: With the development of increasingly reliable automated approaches for the reconstruction of axons and synapses at the EM level, a further speedup of FluoEM is conceivable.
source: Furthermore, with the development of increasingly reliable automated approaches for the reconstruction of axons and synapses at the EM level (Berning et al., 2015; Dorkenwald et al., 2017; Staffler et al., 2017; Januszewski et al., 2018), a further speedup of FluoEM is conceivable in which partially automated matching contributes.
evidence: This is a speculation about future improvements, supported by citations to automation methods.

claim: The presented methods overcome the major hurdle of limited color space for identifying multiple axonal input sources in parallel in large-scale and dense electron microscopic reconstruction of mammalian neuronal circuits.
source: Together, the presented methods overcome the major hurdle of limited color space for identifying multiple axonal input sources in parallel in large-scale and dense electron microscopic reconstruction of mammalian neuronal circuits.
evidence: This is a summary claim about the significance of FluoEM.
